title.zh: 卷六十四 吳書十九 諸葛滕二孫濮陽傳
title.en: Volume 64: Book of Wu 19 - Biographies of Zhuge, Teng, the two Suns, and Puyang
title.raw: 卷六十四 吳書十九 諸葛滕二孫濮陽傳 Volume 64: Book of Wu 19 - Biographies of Zhuge, Teng, the two Suns, and Puyang

sentences.zh: 諸葛恪

translations.literal: Zhuge Ke.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuge Ke

sentences.zh: 諸葛恪字元遜，瑾長子也。

translations.literal: Zhuge Ke, courtesy name Yuansun, was the eldest son of Zhuge Jin.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuge Ke, styled Yuansun, was Zhuge Jin’s eldest son.

sentences.zh: 少知名。

translations.literal: From youth he was known.
translations.idiomatic: He was already celebrated while still young.

sentences.zh: 〈《江表傳》曰：恪少有才名，發藻岐嶷，辯論應機，莫與為對。

translations.literal: The Jiang Biao Zhuan says: From youth Ke had a reputation for talent; he displayed literary brilliance and stood out as precocious; in debate he answered on the instant, and none could match him.
translations.idiomatic: The Jiang Biao Zhuan records that even as a boy Ke was famed for ability: his words were ornate, his mind unusually sharp, and in disputation he met every challenge—no one could best him.

sentences.zh: 權見而奇之，謂瑾曰：「藍田生玉，真不虛也。

translations.literal: Sun Quan saw him and regarded him as extraordinary; he said to Jin, “Jade born at Lantian—the saying is no empty phrase.”
translations.idiomatic: When Sun Quan met him, he was struck by his gifts and told Zhuge Jin, “They were right: fine jade does come from Lantian.”

sentences.zh: 」《吳錄》曰：恪長七尺六寸，少鬚眉，折頞廣額，大口高聲。〉

translations.literal: The Wu lu says: Ke stood seven chi six cun in height, with sparse whiskers and eyebrows, a sharp bridge to his nose and a broad forehead, a large mouth and a loud voice.
translations.idiomatic: The Wu lu adds that he measured seven chi six cun, had thin beard and brows, a prominent nose-bridge and wide forehead, a big mouth, and a carrying voice.

sentences.zh: 弱冠拜騎都尉，與顧譚、張休等侍太子登講論道藝，並為賓友。

translations.literal: Upon reaching the capping age he was appointed Cavalry Commandant; with Gu Tan, Zhang Xiu, and others he attended the heir apparent Deng, lecturing and discussing the Way and the arts, and together they became his guests and friends.
translations.idiomatic: After his capping he became Cavalry Commandant and, alongside Gu Tan and Zhang Xiu, attended Crown Prince Deng to expound the classics and arts; they were counted among the prince’s intimates.

sentences.zh: 從中庶子轉為左輔都尉。

translations.literal: He moved from Palace Attendant to Left Assistant Commandant.
translations.idiomatic: He was transferred from Palace Attendant to Left Assistant Commandant.

sentences.zh: 恪父瑾面長似驢。

translations.literal: Ke's father Jin had a long face like a donkey's.
translations.idiomatic: His father Zhuge Jin had a famously long, donkey-like face.

sentences.zh: 孫權大會群臣，使人牽一驢入，長檢其面，題曰諸葛子瑜。

translations.literal: Sun Quan held a great assembly of ministers and had someone lead in a donkey, attach a tag to its long face, and inscribe it “Zhuge Ziyu.”
translations.idiomatic: At a great court gathering Sun Quan had a donkey led in, a label hung on its long muzzle, and the words “Zhuge Ziyu” written on it.

sentences.zh: 恪跪曰：「乞請竺益兩字。

translations.literal: Ke knelt and said, “I beg leave to add two characters with the brush.”
translations.idiomatic: Zhuge Ke knelt and asked permission to add two brushstrokes to the inscription.

sentences.zh: 」因聽與筆。

translations.literal: Permission was granted and he was given a brush.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Quan assented and handed him the brush.

sentences.zh: 恪績其下曰：「之驢」。

translations.literal: Ke continued the inscription beneath with two characters so that it formed the phrase meaning Zhuge Ziyu’s donkey.
translations.idiomatic: Ke wrote two more characters below so that it read “Zhuge Ziyu’s donkey.”

sentences.zh: 舉座歡笑，乃以驢賜恪。

translations.literal: The whole assembly roared with laughter, and then the donkey was bestowed on Ke.
translations.idiomatic: The hall erupted in laughter, and the donkey was given to Ke.

sentences.zh: 他日復見，權問恪曰：「卿父與叔父孰賢？

translations.literal: Another day when they met again, Sun Quan asked Ke, “Between your father and your uncle, who is the worthier?”
translations.idiomatic: On another occasion Sun Quan asked him, “Which is the better man—your father or your uncle?”

sentences.zh: 」對曰：「臣父為優。

translations.literal: He replied, “My father is the superior.”
translations.idiomatic: “My father,” Ke replied at once.

sentences.zh: 」權問其故。

translations.literal: Sun Quan asked him the reason.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Quan asked why he said so.

sentences.zh: 對曰：「臣父知所事，叔父不知，以是為優。

translations.literal: He replied, “My father knows whom he should serve; my uncle does not; therefore my father is the superior.”
translations.idiomatic: “Because my father understands whom to serve, and my uncle does not—that is why I call him the better man.”

sentences.zh: 」權又大噱。

translations.literal: Sun Quan again roared with laughter.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Quan laughed until he cried.

sentences.zh: 命恪行酒，至張昭前，昭先有酒色，不肯飲。

translations.literal: He ordered Ke to pass the wine; when it came before Zhang Zhao, Zhao was already flushed with wine and refused to drink.
translations.idiomatic: He told Ke to pour for the company; when Ke reached Zhang Zhao, the old minister was already tipsy and would not touch his cup.

sentences.zh: 曰：「此非養老之禮也。

translations.literal: He said, “This is not the courtesy that befits nourishing the old.”
translations.idiomatic: “This,” Zhao protested, “is hardly how one honors age.”

sentences.zh: 」權曰：「卿其能令張公辭屈，乃當飲之耳。

translations.literal: Sun Quan said, “If you can make Lord Zhang concede the argument, then you shall drink.”
translations.idiomatic: Sun Quan said to Ke, “If you can leave Lord Zhang without an answer, you may drink.”

sentences.zh: 」恪難昭曰：「昔師尚父九十，秉旄仗鉞，猶未告老也。

translations.literal: Ke pressed Zhao, saying, “Of old Grand Tutor Shangfu at ninety grasped the banner-axe and still had not announced retirement.”
translations.idiomatic: Ke turned on him: “Grand Tutor Lü Shang was ninety when he took command of the army—he had not yet ‘retired’ then.”

sentences.zh: 今軍旅之事，將軍在後，酒食之事，將軍在先，何謂不養老也？

translations.literal: “Now in matters of army and campaign the general holds the rear; in matters of wine and food the general takes the lead—how can you call that failing to honor old age?”
translations.idiomatic: “In war you hang back; at the feast you are first at the cup—where is the slight to venerable age?”

sentences.zh: 」昭卒無辭，遂為盡爵。

translations.literal: Zhao in the end had no reply, and then he drained his cup.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Zhao had no comeback and emptied his goblet after all.

sentences.zh: 後蜀好，群臣並會，權謂使曰：「此諸葛恪雅使至騎乘，還告丞相，為致好馬。

translations.literal: Later, when relations with Shu were cordial and the ministers all assembled, Sun Quan said to the envoy, “This Zhuge Ke is fond of riding; when you return, tell the Chancellor to send him fine horses.”
translations.idiomatic: Later, at a banquet with Shu envoys present, Sun Quan told the messenger, “Zhuge Ke loves a good mount; ask your chancellor to send him some worthy horses.”

sentences.zh: 」恪因下謝，權曰：「馬未至面謝何也？

translations.literal: Ke thereupon came forward to thank him; Sun Quan said, “The horses have not arrived—why thank me to my face?”
translations.idiomatic: Ke rose to bow his thanks. “The horses are not even here,” said Sun Quan; “why the gratitude already?”

sentences.zh: 」恪對曰：「夫蜀者陛下之外廄，今有恩詔，馬必至也，安敢不謝？

translations.literal: Ke replied, “Shu is Your Majesty’s outer stable; now that Your Majesty has issued this gracious edict, the horses are sure to come—how dare I not give thanks?”
translations.idiomatic: “Shu is Your Majesty’s outer stud,” Ke answered; “once your gracious word goes west, the horses will follow—how could I not thank you?”

sentences.zh: 」恪之才捷，皆此類也。

translations.literal: Ke's quickness of wit was generally of this sort.
translations.idiomatic: His wit was as quick as that in every anecdote above.

sentences.zh: 〈恪別傳曰：權嘗饗蜀使費禕，先逆敕群臣：「使至，伏食勿起。

translations.literal: The Ke Bie Zhuan says: Sun Quan once feasted the Shu envoy Fei Yi and beforehand secretly instructed the ministers, “When the envoy arrives, keep your heads over your bowls and do not rise.”
translations.idiomatic: The separate biography of Ke relates that when Sun Quan feasted Fei Yi of Shu, he secretly told his officials, “Stay seated over your food when the envoy enters.”

sentences.zh: 」禕至，權為輟食，而群下不起。

translations.literal: When Fei Yi arrived, Sun Quan for his part stopped eating, but those below did not rise.
translations.idiomatic: Fei Yi came in; Sun Quan set down his chopsticks, yet none of the ministers stood.

sentences.zh: 禕啁之曰：「鳳皇來翔，騏驎吐哺，驢騾無知，伏食如故。

translations.literal: Fei Yi mocked them, saying, “When the phoenix alights and the qilin spits food [to welcome a worthy], donkeys and mules, knowing nothing, keep their heads over their food as before.”
translations.idiomatic: Fei Yi quipped, “Where the phoenix lands and the unicorn ‘spits its food,’ mules and donkeys simply go on munching, heads down, none the wiser.”

sentences.zh: 」恪答曰：「爰植梧桐，以待鳳皇，有何燕雀，自稱來翔？

translations.literal: Ke answered, “We have planted the parasol tree to await the phoenix—what sort of sparrows and swallows dare call themselves ‘alighting in flight’?”
translations.idiomatic: Ke shot back, “We planted the wutong to court the phoenix—what business have common sparrows claiming they ‘come in state’?”

sentences.zh: 何不彈射，使還故鄉！

translations.literal: “Why not shoot them away and send them back where they came from?”
translations.idiomatic: “Someone ought to string a bow and drive them home to their nests.”

sentences.zh: 」禕停食餅，索筆作麥賦，恪亦請筆作磨賦，咸稱善焉。

translations.literal: Fei Yi put down his cake, asked for a brush, and composed an “Ode to Wheat”; Ke likewise asked for a brush and composed an “Ode to the Millstone,” and all praised them.
translations.idiomatic: Fei Yi laid aside a wheat cake, borrowed a brush, and wrote an “Ode to Wheat”; Ke borrowed a brush too and answered with an “Ode to the Millstone,” to general applause.

sentences.zh: 權嘗問恪：「頃何以自娛，而更肥澤？

translations.literal: Sun Quan once asked Ke, “What lately have you been doing to amuse yourself, that you grow plumper and sleeker?”
translations.idiomatic: Sun Quan teased him another time: “What have you been doing for pleasure—you look sleeker than ever.”

sentences.zh: 」恪對曰：「臣聞富潤屋，德潤身，臣非敢自娛，脩己而已。

translations.literal: Ke replied, “I have heard that wealth adorns the house and virtue adorns the person; I do not presume to amuse myself—I merely cultivate myself.”
translations.idiomatic: “They say riches polish a hall and virtue polishes the man,” said Ke; “I am not amusing myself—I am only trying to improve.”

sentences.zh: 」又問：「卿何如滕胤？

translations.literal: He asked again, “How do you compare to Teng Yin?”
translations.idiomatic: “How do you measure against Teng Yin?” Sun Quan went on.

sentences.zh: 」恪答曰：「登階躡履，臣不如胤；

translations.literal: Ke answered, “Mounting steps and adjusting my slippers—I am not Yin’s equal;
translations.idiomatic: “For mounting the steps and minding small decorum,” Ke said, “I am no match for Teng Yin;

sentences.zh: 回籌轉策，胤不如臣。

translations.literal: in turning strategies on the counting-rods, Yin is not my equal.”
translations.idiomatic: but for spinning plans behind the curtain, Teng Yin is no match for me.”

sentences.zh: 」恪嘗獻權馬，先钅芻其耳。

translations.literal: Once when Ke presented a horse to Sun Quan, he first had its ears notched.
translations.idiomatic: On one occasion Ke presented a horse to the throne after first notching its ears.

sentences.zh: 範慎時在坐，嘲恪曰：「馬雖大畜，禀氣於天，今殘其耳，豈不傷仁？

translations.literal: Fan Shen was present and taunted Ke, saying, “Though a horse is a great domestic animal, it draws its qi from Heaven; now you mutilate its ears—is that not an injury to benevolence?”
translations.idiomatic: Fan Shen, who was there, needled him: “A horse is a noble creature, heaven’s gift; to maim its ears—does that not wound humaneness?”

sentences.zh: 」恪答曰：「母之於女，恩愛至矣，穿耳附珠，何傷於仁？

translations.literal: Ke answered, “A mother toward her daughter loves her utterly; yet she pierces her ears to hang pearls—where is the harm to benevolence?”
translations.idiomatic: Ke retorted, “Mothers love their daughters dearly, yet they bore their ears for pearls—where is the harm to humaneness in that?”

sentences.zh: 」太子嘗嘲恪：「諸葛元遜可食馬矢。

translations.literal: The heir apparent once teased Ke, “Zhuge Yuansun ought to eat horse dung.”
translations.idiomatic: The crown prince once joked, “Someone ought to feed Zhuge Yuansun horse droppings.”

sentences.zh: 」恪曰：「原太子食雞卵。

translations.literal: Ke said, “Then let the heir apparent eat chicken eggs.”
translations.idiomatic: “Then let His Highness dine on eggs,” said Ke.

sentences.zh: 」權曰：「人令卿食馬矢，卿使人食雞卵何也？

translations.literal: Sun Quan said, “He told you to eat horse dung—why do you tell him to eat eggs?”
translations.idiomatic: Sun Quan asked, “He told you to eat dung; why do you tell him to eat eggs?”

sentences.zh: 」恪曰：「所出同耳。

translations.literal: Ke said, “They come from the same place.”
translations.idiomatic: “They come from the same place,” Ke replied evenly.

sentences.zh: 」權大笑。

translations.literal: Sun Quan burst out laughing.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor roared with laughter.

sentences.zh: 《江表傳》曰：曾有白頭鳥集殿前，權曰：「此何鳥也？

translations.literal: The Jiang Biao Zhuan says: Once a white-headed bird perched before the hall, and Sun Quan said, “What bird is this?”
translations.idiomatic: The Jiang Biao Zhuan tells how a white-headed wagtail lit on the palace steps; Sun Quan asked what bird it was.

sentences.zh: 」恪曰：「白頭翁也。

translations.literal: Ke said, “It is a white-headed old man (wagtail).”
translations.idiomatic: “A white-headed wagtail,” said Ke—the name is a pun on “white-haired old man.”

sentences.zh: 」張昭自以坐中最老，疑恪以鳥戲之，因曰：「恪欺陛下，未嘗聞鳥名白頭翁者，試使恪复求白頭母。

translations.literal: Zhang Zhao, thinking himself the eldest at the table, suspected Ke was mocking him with the bird, and said, “Ke deceives Your Majesty; I have never heard of a bird called ‘white-headed old man’—let Ke try to produce a white-headed mother as well.”
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Zhao, eldest in the company, thought himself the butt of the joke and said, “Ke is fooling Your Majesty—there is no such bird; let him produce a ‘white-headed mother’ if he can.”

sentences.zh: 」恪曰：「鳥名鸚母，未必有對，試使輔吳复求鸚父。

translations.literal: Ke said, “There is a bird called ‘parrot mother’; it need not have a mate—let Lord Fuwu try to produce a parrot father too.”
translations.idiomatic: “There is a ‘mother parrot’ without any sure ‘father parrot,’” Ke answered; “shall we ask Lord Fuwu to fetch a ‘parrot father’?”

sentences.zh: 」昭不能答，坐中皆歡笑。〉

translations.literal: Zhao could not reply, and the whole company laughed.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Zhao had no answer, and the whole hall rocked with laughter.

sentences.zh: 權甚異之，欲試以事，令守節度。

translations.literal: Sun Quan marveled at him greatly and wished to try him with responsibility, assigning him to hold the post of Controller.
translations.idiomatic: So impressed was Sun Quan that he decided to test Ke with real duty and put him in charge of the Controller’s office.

sentences.zh: 節度掌軍糧谷，文書繁猥，非其好也。

translations.literal: The Controller managed army grain; paperwork was tangled and oppressive, and it was not to his liking.
translations.idiomatic: That office handled army grain and endless paperwork—work Ke found uncongenial.

sentences.zh: 〈《江表傳》曰：權為吳王，初置節度官，使典掌軍糧，非漢制也。

translations.literal: The Jiang Biao Zhuan says: When Sun Quan became King of Wu, he first established the office of Controller to supervise army grain; it was not a Han institution.
translations.idiomatic: The Jiang Biao Zhuan notes that when Sun Quan became King of Wu he created the Controller post for grain supply—something the Han never had.

sentences.zh: 初用侍中偏將軍徐詳，詳死，將用恪。

translations.literal: At first he had appointed Palace Attendant and Major-General Xu Xiang; when Xiang died, he was about to appoint Ke.
translations.idiomatic: The first holder had been Palace Attendant Xu Xiang; when Xu died, Ke was slated to succeed him.

sentences.zh: 諸葛亮聞恪代詳，書與陸遜曰：「家兄年老，而恪性疏，今使典主糧穀，糧穀軍之要最，僕雖在遠，竊用不安。

translations.literal: Zhuge Liang, hearing that Ke would replace Xiang, wrote to Lu Xun: “My elder brother is advanced in years, while Ke’s nature is heedless; now to have him oversee grain—grain is the vital core of an army—though I am far away, I cannot help but be uneasy.”
translations.idiomatic: Zhuge Liang, learning that Ke would take the post, wrote Lu Xun: “My brother is old, and Ke is careless by nature; grain is the army’s lifeblood—though I am far off, I am privately uneasy at his managing it.”

sentences.zh: 足下特為啟至尊轉之。

translations.literal: “Would you especially petition the August Supreme One to transfer him to another post?”
translations.idiomatic: “Please speak to the sovereign for me and have him reassigned.”

sentences.zh: 」遜以白權，即轉恪領兵。〉

translations.literal: Lu Xun reported this to Sun Quan, who thereupon transferred Ke to command troops.
translations.idiomatic: Lu Xun relayed the plea, and Sun Quan immediately moved Ke to a field command.

sentences.zh: 恪以丹楊山險，民多果勁，雖前發兵，徒得外縣平民而已。

translations.literal: Ke held that Danyang's mountains were precipitous and its people bold and hardy; though troops had been sent out before, they had obtained only the commoners of the outer counties.
translations.idiomatic: Ke argued that Danyang’s mountains bred a tough, warlike people: past expeditions had cleared only the lowland towns, never the heartland.

sentences.zh: 其餘深遠，莫能禽盡，屢自求乞為官出之。

translations.literal: The rest in the remote depths could not be seized and eliminated; he repeatedly begged on his own initiative to go forth as an official and flush them out.
translations.idiomatic: The deep hills remained beyond reach; he therefore begged again and again to be sent in person to dig them out.

sentences.zh: 三年可得甲士四萬。

translations.literal: “In three years one could obtain forty thousand armored soldiers.”
translations.idiomatic: He promised forty thousand armored men within three years.

sentences.zh: 眾議咸以「丹楊地勢險阻，與吳郡、會稽、新都、鄱陽四郡鄰接，周旋數千里，山谷萬重，其幽邃民人，未嘗人城邑，對長吏，皆仗兵野逸，白首於林莽。

translations.literal: The assembly all said: “Danyang’s terrain is rugged; it adjoins Wu, Kuaiji, Xindu, and Poyang commanderies over several thousand li, with myriad folds of valley; the people in its hidden recesses have never entered walled towns or faced a magistrate; all go armed in the wilds and grow white-haired in the brush.”
translations.idiomatic: Court opinion ran: “Danyang is a maze of ridges touching Wu, Kuaiji, Xindu, and Poyang across thousands of li; its hidden dwellers never see a yamen or a magistrate—they live and die armed in the hills.”

sentences.zh: 逋亡宿惡，咸共逃竄。

translations.literal: Fugitives and habitual criminals alike fled there together.
translations.idiomatic: Fugitives and hardened bandits alike fled into those fastnesses.

sentences.zh: 山出銅鐵，自鑄甲兵。

translations.literal: The mountains yield copper and iron, and they cast armor and weapons themselves.
translations.idiomatic: The hills yield copper and iron, so they forge their own arms.

sentences.zh: 俗好武習戰，高尚氣力，其升山赴險，抵突叢棘。

translations.literal: Their customs favor arms and drill in war; they esteem raw strength; they climb mountains and brave passes, butting through thickets.
translations.idiomatic: They love fighting and prize brute strength; they scale cliffs and charge thickets

sentences.zh: 若魚之走淵，猿狖之騰木也。

translations.literal: They are like fish darting into pools or gibbons leaping through the trees.
translations.idiomatic: like fish diving for the deeps or apes vaulting through the canopy.

sentences.zh: 時觀間隙，出為寇盜，每致兵征伐，尋其窟藏。

translations.literal: Watching for openings, they issue forth as bandits; whenever troops are raised to subdue them, one must seek their lairs.
translations.idiomatic: They watch for slack moments to raid the lowlands, and whenever armies march in, they melt away to secret lairs.

sentences.zh: 其戰則蜂至，敗則鳥竄，自前世以來，不能羈也」。

translations.literal: “In battle they swarm like bees; in defeat they scatter like birds—since antiquity they have never been brought to heel.”
translations.idiomatic: “They swarm like bees when you fight and vanish like birds when you lose—no dynasty has ever truly tamed them.”

sentences.zh: 皆以為難。

translations.literal: All thought it difficult.
translations.idiomatic: Everyone called the scheme impracticable.

sentences.zh: 恪父瑾聞之，亦以事終不逮，歎曰：「恪不大興吾家，將大赤吾族也。

translations.literal: Ke’s father Jin, hearing of it, also judged that the affair would not ultimately succeed and sighed, “If Ke does not greatly exalt our clan, he will utterly destroy it.”
translations.idiomatic: When Zhuge Jin heard the plan, he judged it beyond success and sighed, “This boy will either make our house or ruin our whole clan.”

sentences.zh: 」恪盛陳其必捷。

translations.literal: Ke forcefully insisted that victory was certain.
translations.idiomatic: Ke only pressed his certainty of success all the harder.

sentences.zh: 權拜恪撫趙將軍，領丹楊太守，授棨戟武騎三百。

translations.literal: Sun Quan appointed Ke General Who Pacifies Zhao, concurrent Governor of Danyang, and gave him three hundred halberd-bearing armed riders.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Quan named him General Who Pacifies Zhao, Governor of Danyang, and assigned him three hundred halberd guards.

sentences.zh: 拜畢，命恪備威儀，作鼓吹，導引歸家，時年三十二。

translations.literal: When the investiture was done, he ordered Ke to array full honors, set up drums and pipes, and escort him home; Ke was thirty-two at the time.
translations.idiomatic: After the audience Sun Quan had him escorted home with full music and panoply of honor; Ke was thirty-two.

sentences.zh: 恪到府，乃移書四部屬城長空。

translations.literal: When Ke reached headquarters, he then sent notices to the magistrates of the cities subordinate to the four divisions (the transmitted graphs here are corrupt).
translations.idiomatic: Once installed at his seat, he wrote to every district magistrate under the four circuits.

sentences.zh: 令各保其疆界，明立部伍，其從化平民，悉令屯居。

translations.literal: He ordered each to secure his borders and clearly establish companies; commoners who submitted to civilizing rule were all ordered to settle in garrison colonies.
translations.idiomatic: Each was to hold his border, drill his companies, and move compliant commoners into guarded settlements.

sentences.zh: 乃分內諸將，羅兵幽阻，但繕藩籬，不與交鋒，候其穀稼將熟，輒縱兵芟刈，使無遺種。

translations.literal: He then assigned his generals within the command, strung troops along the hidden defiles, but only repaired palisades and did not join battle; when the grain crops were nearly ripe, he repeatedly sent troops to reap and cut them down, leaving no seed.
translations.idiomatic: He spread his officers through the defiles with palisades but no pitched battles, then sent parties to strip the mountain fields whenever the grain ripened, leaving nothing to harvest.

sentences.zh: 舊谷既盡，新田不收，平民屯居，略無所入，於是山民饑窮，漸出降首。

translations.literal: When old grain was exhausted and new fields yielded no harvest, and the garrisoned commoners had scarcely any income, the mountain folk grew hungry and desperate and gradually came out to surrender.
translations.idiomatic: When the old stores were gone and the new crop never came in, the hill folk starved and drifted down in twos and threes to yield.

sentences.zh: 恪乃復敕下曰：「山民去惡從化，皆當撫慰，徙出外縣，不得嫌疑，有所執拘。

translations.literal: Ke then issued orders again, saying, “Mountain people who cast off evil and follow civilization must all be comforted and resettled in outer counties; none may harbor suspicions or seize and bind them.”
translations.idiomatic: Ke then proclaimed that every mountaineer who came in good faith was to be fed, resettled downstream, and never harassed on suspicion.

sentences.zh: 」臼陽長胡伉得降民周遺，遺舊惡民，困迫暫出，內圖叛逆，伉縛送言府。

translations.literal: The magistrate of Jiuyang, Hu Kang, took a surrendered man Zhou Yi; Yi was an old habitual wrongdoer who had come out only from distress and inwardly plotted rebellion; Kang bound him and sent him to report at headquarters.
translations.idiomatic: Hu Kang, magistrate of Jiuyang, bound a new surrender named Zhou Yi—a known villain who meant to rebel—and sent him up to headquarters.

sentences.zh: 恪以伉違教，遂斬以徇，以狀表上。

translations.literal: Ke, holding that Kang had violated the order, then had him beheaded as a public warning and memorialized the facts to the throne.
translations.idiomatic: Ke judged that a breach of his order and had Hu Kang executed as a warning, then reported the matter in a memorial.

sentences.zh: 民聞伉坐執人被戮，知官惟欲出之而已，於是老幼相攜而出，歲期，人數皆如本規。

translations.literal: When the people heard that Kang had been executed for detaining a surrender, they understood that the officials only wished to draw them out; old and young then came forth hand in hand, and by the year’s end the headcount matched the original plan.
translations.idiomatic: When the hill people learned that Hu Kang died merely for seizing a surrender, they understood the government only wanted them out; whole villages came down, and within a year the tallies matched Ke’s original pledge.

sentences.zh: 恪自領萬人，餘分給諸將。

translations.literal: Ke personally led ten thousand men; the remainder he distributed among the various generals.
translations.idiomatic: Ke himself commanded ten thousand men and parceled the rest among his generals.

sentences.zh: 權嘉其功，遣尚書僕射薛綜勞軍。

translations.literal: Sun Quan commended his achievement and sent Vice Director of the Secretariat Xue Zong to reward the army.
translations.idiomatic: Delighted with the result, Sun Quan sent Vice Director Xue Zong of the Secretariat to commend the troops.

sentences.zh: 綜先移恪等曰：

translations.literal: Zong first sent a communication to Ke and the others, saying:
translations.idiomatic: Xue Zong first addressed Ke and his officers in a written message:

sentences.zh: 山越恃阻，不賓歷世，緩則首鼠，急則狼顧。

translations.literal: The Shanyue rely on their barriers and have not submitted for generations; when treated leniently they hesitate like a rat with two heads, when pressed hard they glance about like a wolf.
translations.idiomatic: For ages the Shanyue have defied the throne from their strongholds—pamper them and they dither; corner them and they wheel like wolves.

sentences.zh: 皇帝赫然，命將西征，神策內授，武師外震。

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven blazed with wrath, ordered a general to march west, divine plans were given within, martial hosts thundered without.
translations.idiomatic: The sovereign’s wrath flashed like lightning; generals marched west while secret stratagems were hatched within and armies thundered on every border.

sentences.zh: 兵不染鍔，甲不沾汗。

translations.literal: Weapons were not stained on their edges, armor did not grow damp with sweat.
translations.idiomatic: Blades never tasted blood; corselets never ran with sweat—a bloodless triumph.

sentences.zh: 元惡既梟，種黨歸義，蕩滌山藪，獻戎十萬。

translations.literal: The chief villain was beheaded; all factions submitted in righteousness; the mountain fastnesses were scoured, and a hundred thousand captives were presented.
translations.idiomatic: The ringleaders lost their heads, their followers sued for peace, the hills were swept clean, and a hundred thousand fighters were delivered to the rolls.

sentences.zh: 野無遺寇，邑罔殘姦。

translations.literal: In the wilds no bandit remains; in the towns no villain stalks.
translations.idiomatic: The countryside is clear of raiders; the towns hold no lurking traitors.

sentences.zh: 既掃兇慝，又充軍用。

translations.literal: You have swept away the vicious and also filled the army’s needs.
translations.idiomatic: You have purged evil and at the same time stocked the camps.

sentences.zh: 藜筱稂莠，化為善草。

translations.literal: Brambles and tares have turned into good pasturage.
translations.idiomatic: Thorns and weeds have turned into good grazing ground.

sentences.zh: 魑魅魍魎，更成虎土。

translations.literal: Sprites and goblins have become tiger guards.
translations.idiomatic: Forest demons have been forged into crack troops.

sentences.zh: 雖實國家威靈之所加，亦信無帥臨履之所致也。

translations.literal: Though this is indeed where the state’s awesome numen was brought to bear, it is also truly because the commander-in-chief went in person.
translations.idiomatic: Credit belongs to Heaven’s favor on the dynasty, yet it is no less the fruit of a field commander who went among the rocks himself.

sentences.zh: 雖《詩》美執訊，《易》嘉折首，週之方、召，漢之衛、霍，豈足以談？

translations.literal: Though the Odes praise taking captives, the Changes honors beheading the chief—even the Fang and Shao of Zhou, the Wei and Huo of Han—are they worth mentioning?
translations.idiomatic: The Odes may hymn “bringing prisoners,” the Changes may bless “striking the chief,” yet even Fang and Shao of Zhou or Wei Qing and Huo Qubing of Han scarcely bear comparison.

sentences.zh: 功軼古人，勳超前世。

translations.literal: Your merit surpasses the ancients; your deeds outstrip earlier ages.
translations.idiomatic: Your achievement outruns the ancients; your fame eclipses former generations.

sentences.zh: 主上歡然，遙用歎息。

translations.literal: The sovereign rejoices and, from afar, sighs with admiration.
translations.idiomatic: The throne rejoices and, though miles away, murmurs praise.

sentences.zh: 感《四牡》之遺典，思飲至之舊章。

translations.literal: He is moved by the enduring precedent of “Four Steeds” and recalls the old rites of the drink-on-arrival feast.
translations.idiomatic: He thinks of the “Four Steeds” ode and longs to feast you by the old “victory cup” rite.

sentences.zh: 故遣中台近官，迎致稿賜，以旌茂功，以慰劬勞。

translations.literal: Hence he sends a close attendant from the Central Terrace to welcome you with grain bounty and gifts, to honor your splendid merit and comfort your weary toil.
translations.idiomatic: So he dispatches an intimate minister from the central secretariat with grain largesse and gifts—to crown your merit and soothe your weary hosts.

sentences.zh: 拜恪威北將軍，封都鄉侯。

translations.literal: Ke was appointed General Who Awes the North and enfeoffed as marquis of Duxiang canton.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuge Ke was promoted to General Who Awes the North and given the village-marquisate of Duxiang.

sentences.zh: 恪乞率眾佃廬江皖口，因輕兵襲舒，掩得其民而還。

translations.literal: Ke requested to lead the troops to open farms at Wan Mouth in Lujiang, then with light forces raid Shu, overrun it by surprise, seize the populace, and withdraw.
translations.idiomatic: He asked to colonize the fields at Wan Mouth in Lujiang, then strike Shu with a flying column, scoop up the people, and retire before Wei could react.

sentences.zh: 復遠遣斥候，觀相徑要，欲圖壽春，權以為不可。

translations.literal: He again sent scouts far ahead to reconnoiter roads and chokepoints, intending to move against Shouchun; Sun Quan judged it imprudent.
translations.idiomatic: He pushed scouts deeper to map approaches toward Shouchun, but the sovereign forbade the gamble.

sentences.zh: 赤烏中，魏司馬宣王謀欲攻恪。

translations.literal: During the Chiwu reign-period, Sima Yi (King Xuan of Wei) planned an offensive against Ke.
translations.idiomatic: In the Chiwu years Sima Yi of Wei laid plans to crush Zhuge Ke.

sentences.zh: 權方發兵應之，望氣者以為不利，於是徒恪屯於柴桑。

translations.literal: Sun Quan was on the point of raising troops to counter him when specialists in reading vapors pronounced the omens ill; thereupon Ke’s command was shifted to garrison Chaisang.
translations.idiomatic: Wu was mobilizing to meet the threat when court diviners called the stars hostile, so Ke’s corps was redeployed to Chaisang.

sentences.zh: 與丞相陸遜書曰：

translations.literal: He wrote to Chancellor Lu Xun, saying:
translations.idiomatic: He sent Chancellor Lu Xun a letter that ran:

sentences.zh: 楊敬叔傳述清論，以為方今人物凋盡，守德業者不能復幾，宜相左右。

translations.literal: Yang Jingshu’s tract relays the Pure Critique, holding that men of real stature are now exhausted—those who guard virtue can scarcely be numbered—and urged mutual support.
translations.idiomatic: Yang Jingshu’s essay repeats the “pure conversation” line that talent has thinned to nothing and men of principle must lean on one another.

sentences.zh: 更為輔車，上熙國事，下相珍惜。

translations.literal: Become axle-cogs for each other: brighten affairs of state above and cherish one another below.
translations.idiomatic: They should lock shields—advance the kingdom upstairs and watch each other’s backs downstairs.

sentences.zh: 又疾世俗好相謗毀，使已成之器，中有損累。

translations.literal: He also deplored vulgar habit of mutual slander, which mars finished vessels from within.
translations.idiomatic: He hated how fashionable spite chips cracks into men already shaped for office.

sentences.zh: 將進之徒，意不歡笑，聞此喟然，誠獨擊節。

translations.literal: Men poised for promotion grow grim instead of glad; hearing this they sigh and alone beat time in assent.
translations.idiomatic: Men on the verge of advance heard him and sighed, secretly applauding every beat.

sentences.zh: 愚以為君子不求備於一人，自孔氏門徒大數三幹，其見者七十二人。

translations.literal: I deem it wrong for the gentleman to demand completeness in any single man; even Confucius’ disciples numbered near three thousand, yet those actually seen numbered seventy-two.
translations.idiomatic: A gentleman does not ask one man for perfection: Confucius taught nearly three thousand, yet only seventy-two stood out.

sentences.zh: 至於子張、子路、子貢等七十之徒，亞聖之德，然猶各有所短，師闢由喭，賜不受命，豈況下此而無所闕？

translations.literal: As for Zizhang, Zilu, Zigong, and the rest of the seventy—men next only to the Sage—they still each had his flaw; the Master faulted You for rashness and Xi for refusing orders—how much more must lesser men show gaps?
translations.idiomatic: Among the seventy luminaries next to the Sage, Zizhang was reckless, Zilu blunt, Zigong headstrong—if they fell short, who beneath them does not?

sentences.zh: 且仲尼不以數予之不備而引以為友，不以人所短棄其所長也。

translations.literal: Moreover Zhongni did not spurn Zihua’s incompleteness but drew him as a friend, nor cast away men’s strength on account of their weakness.
translations.idiomatic: Confucius never dismissed Gongxi Zihua for lacking polish; he prized gifts and forgave faults.

sentences.zh: 加以當今取士，宜寬於往古，何者？

translations.literal: Add that selecting officers today ought to be more generous than in antiquity—why?
translations.idiomatic: Today’s recruitment must be broader than the ancients’—why?

sentences.zh: 時務從橫，而善人單少，國家職司，常苦不充。

translations.literal: Affairs rush crosswise while good men are few; state offices constantly groan under vacancies.
translations.idiomatic: The age twists every which way and worthy men are scarce; every ministry runs short-handed.

sentences.zh: 苟令性不邪惡，志在陳力，便可獎就，騁其所任。

translations.literal: If nature be not vicious and the will bent on serving with strength, encourage and employ him—give rein to whatever office fits.
translations.idiomatic: Whoever is honest and eager to serve should be lifted up and tried at the post that suits him.

sentences.zh: 若於小小宜適，私行不足，皆宜闊略，不足縷責。

translations.literal: Where petty tact or private conduct falls short, overlook it in breadth—do not pick every loose thread.
translations.idiomatic: Small lapses in manners or private life should slide—do not haul men over the coals for trivia.

sentences.zh: 且士誠不可纖論苛克，苛克則彼賢聖猶將不全，況其出入者邪？

translations.literal: Moreover gentlemen truly cannot be weighed on hair-splitting scales; hair-splitting would leave even sages incomplete—how much more ordinary men?
translations.idiomatic: Perfectionism would indict even sages; how shall middling talents escape it?

sentences.zh: 故曰以道望人則難，以人望人則易，賢愚可知。

translations.literal: Hence the saying: demanding others by the Way is hard; judging others as fellow humans is easy—the worthy and foolish sort themselves.
translations.idiomatic: So the proverb runs: judge by the Way and no one passes; judge as men and merit shows plain.

sentences.zh: 自漢末以來，中國土大夫如許子將輩，所以更相謗訕，或至為禍，原其本起。

translations.literal: Since late Han, gentlemen of the interior such as Xu Zijiang traded barbed appraisals until some brought disaster—trace it to the root.
translations.idiomatic: Since Han fell, salon critics like Xu Shao slandered each other into ruin—consider where that began.

sentences.zh: 非為大仇，惟坐克己不能盡如禮，而責人專以正義。

translations.literal: It was no mortal feud—only that they could not themselves fulfill ritual in every detail yet demanded others bow to abstract righteousness.
translations.idiomatic: They were not mortal enemies—only hypocrites who failed the rites themselves yet preached righteousness at others.

sentences.zh: 夫己不如禮，則人不服。

translations.literal: When oneself falls short of ritual, others will not submit.
translations.idiomatic: Fault yourself before the rites and men withhold respect.

sentences.zh: 責人以正義，則人不堪。

translations.literal: Demand righteousness of others and they cannot bear it.
translations.idiomatic: Hammer others with moral absolutes and they break.

sentences.zh: 內不服其行，外不堪其責，則不得不相怨。

translations.literal: Within they refuse your conduct; without they choke on your blame—then mutual resentment becomes inevitable.
translations.idiomatic: They resent your example and your lecture alike—bad blood follows.

sentences.zh: 相怨一生，則小人得容其間。

translations.literal: Once resentment lasts a lifetime, petty men find room to wedge between.
translations.idiomatic: Give spite a lifetime and sneak thieves slip between you.

sentences.zh: 得容其間，則三至之言，浸潤之譖，紛錯交至。

translations.literal: Once wedges appear, thrice-told slanders and soaking whisper-calumnies arrive in a tangle.
translations.idiomatic: Then “third-hearing” lies and slow-poison gossip pile up together.

sentences.zh: 雖使至明至親者處之，猶難以自定。

translations.literal: Though the clearest sight and closest kin sit between them, they still can hardly steady themselves.
translations.idiomatic: Even the keenest eye and dearest blood tie cannot steady such storms.

sentences.zh: 況已為隙，且未能明者乎？

translations.literal: How much less when rifts already yawn and clarity has failed?
translations.idiomatic: How much worse once the breach is open and neither side sees straight?

sentences.zh: 是故張、陳至於血刃，蕭、朱不終其好，本由於此而已。

translations.literal: Hence Zhang Er and Chen Yu came to blades drawn; Xiao Yu and Zhu Bo ended their friendship—the root was only this.
translations.idiomatic: So Zhang Er and Chen Yu drew steel; Xiao Wangzhi and Zhu Bo parted—for no deeper cause than this.

sentences.zh: 夫不捨小過，纖微相責，久乃至於家戶為怨，一國無復全行之士也。

translations.literal: If small faults are not waived and pinpricks accumulate, in time every household nurses a grudge and no whole man walks the realm.
translations.idiomatic: Nurse every nick and soon whole clans feud—no court then holds an intact gentleman.

sentences.zh: 恪知遜以此嫌己，故遂廣其理而贊其旨也。

translations.literal: Ke knew Lu Xun therefore bore him a grudge, and so expanded these principles to endorse Lu’s intent.
translations.idiomatic: Knowing Lu Xun suspected him, Ke spun out this argument to echo Lu’s own plea for tolerance.

sentences.zh: 會遜卒，恪遷大將軍，假節，駐武昌，代遜領荊州事。

translations.literal: When Lu Xun died, Ke was promoted Grand General, granted credential insignia, stationed at Wuchang, and succeeded Xun in directing Jingzhou affairs.
translations.idiomatic: Lu Xun’s death vaulted Ke to Grand General with battle authority at Wuchang, inheriting the western theater.

sentences.zh: 久之，權不豫，而太子少，乃徵恪以大將軍領太子太傅，中書令孫弘領少傅。

translations.literal: After a long while Sun Quan fell ill while the heir was still young; he therefore summoned Ke to serve as Grand General concurrent Mentor to the Heir Apparent, with Palace Secretariat Director Sun Hong as Junior Mentor.
translations.idiomatic: When age and illness gripped Sun Quan while the crown prince remained a boy, he recalled Ke as Grand General and tutor to the heir, pairing him with Sun Hong as junior tutor.

sentences.zh: 權疾困，召恪、弘及太常滕胤、將軍呂據、侍中孫峻，屬以後事。

translations.literal: As Sun Quan’s illness turned grave he summoned Ke, Hong, Chamberlain for Ceremonies Teng Yin, general Lü Ju, and attendant Sun Jun and entrusted them with what should follow his death.
translations.idiomatic: On his deathbed he called Ke, Hong, Teng Yin, Lü Ju, and Sun Jun to settle the succession.

sentences.zh: 〈《吳書》曰：權寢疾，議所付託。

translations.literal: The Wu shu says: When Sun Quan took to his sickbed, court debated whom to entrust.
translations.idiomatic: The Wu shu records that as the emperor sickened, ministers wrangled over the regency.

sentences.zh: 時朝臣咸皆注意於恪，而孫峻表恪器任輔政，可付大事。

translations.literal: At the time every minister looked to Ke, while Sun Jun memorialized that Ke’s talent fitted chief counselor duty and great affairs could be committed to him.
translations.idiomatic: All eyes fell on Ke; Sun Jun alone filed a memorial that Ke could shoulder the regency.

sentences.zh: 權嫌恪剛很自用，峻以當今朝臣皆莫及，遂固保之，乃徵恪。

translations.literal: Sun Quan distrusted Ke’s stubbornness and self-will, but Jun argued that none among current ministers matched him; pressing the point, he secured Quan’s consent and Ke was summoned.
translations.idiomatic: Quan hesitated—Ke was harsh and headstrong—but Jun insisted no present minister surpassed him and talked the sovereign round.

sentences.zh: 後引恪等見臥內，受詔床下，權詔曰：「吾疾困矣，恐不復相見，諸事一以相委。

translations.literal: Later Quan led Ke and the others into his bedchamber; beneath the couch they received edict, and Quan’s decree ran: “My illness is desperate; I fear we shall not meet again—all affairs I wholly delegate.
translations.idiomatic: He drew them to his bedside and said from the pallet, “I am dying; we may not speak again—everything rests with you.”

sentences.zh: 」恪歔欷流涕曰：「臣等皆受厚恩，當以死奉詔，原陛下安精神，損思慮，無以外事為念。

translations.literal: Ke sobbed and wept, saying, “We have all received overwhelming grace and shall obey the edict unto death; may Your Majesty calm your spirit and ease your cares—think no more of outward matters.”
translations.idiomatic: Ke wept and vowed to spend his life on the charge, begging Quan to rest easy and leave the world behind.

sentences.zh: 」權詔有司諸事一統於恪，惟殺生大事然後以聞。

translations.literal: Quan ordered the bureaus that every matter report first to Ke; only decisions on life and death should then be brought to the throne.
translations.idiomatic: Ordinance followed: all routine went to Ke; capital sentences alone reached the palace.

sentences.zh: 為治第館，設陪衛。

translations.literal: A mansion was built for him with attendant guards.
translations.idiomatic: They raised him a residence ringed by household troops.

sentences.zh: 群官百司拜揖之儀，各有品敘。

translations.literal: The bows and courtesies owed him by the hundred offices each followed graded precedence.
translations.idiomatic: Every agency received scripted ritual for greeting the regent.

sentences.zh: 諸法令有不便者，條列以聞，權輒聽之。

translations.literal: Where statutes proved cumbersome, Ke should list them in memorial and Quan always approved.
translations.idiomatic: Awkward laws went up on Ke’s list and Quan rubber-stamped the fixes.

sentences.zh: 中外翕然，人懷歡欣。〉

translations.literal: Inside and outside fell into calm; men walked with joy.
translations.idiomatic: Court and countryside breathed relief—hope after dread.

sentences.zh: 翌日，權薨。

translations.literal: The next day Sun Quan died.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Quan died the following dawn.

sentences.zh: 弘素與恪不平，懼為恪所治，秘權死問，欲矯詔除恪。

translations.literal: Hong had long been at odds with Ke and feared Ke would punish him; he concealed news of Quan’s death and plotted a forged edict to dismiss Ke.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Hong, Ke’s enemy, hid the death and drafted a false order to purge him.

sentences.zh: 峻以告恪，恪請弘諮事，於坐中誅之，乃發喪制服。

translations.literal: Jun informed Ke; Ke summoned Hong on official business and slew him in session, then published mourning and donned hemp.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Jun tipped Ke; Ke invited Hong to council and cut him down mid-meeting, then proclaimed the obsequies.

sentences.zh: 與弟公安督融書曰：

translations.literal: He wrote to his younger brother Rong, colonel at Gongan, saying:
translations.idiomatic: He wrote his brother Zhuge Rong, defender of Gongan:

sentences.zh: 今月十六日乙未，大行皇帝委棄萬國，群下大小，莫不傷悼。

translations.literal: On the sixteenth of this month, yiwei, the late emperor relinquished the myriad regions; high and low alike mourn.
translations.idiomatic: The sixteenth, day yiwei—the Great Late Emperor has left the realm; every rank weeps.

sentences.zh: 至吾父子兄弟，井受殊恩，非徒凡庸之隸，是以悲慟，肝心圮裂。

translations.literal: As for our father and sons and brothers, we received singular favor—we are no common hirelings; hence our grief splits the liver.
translations.idiomatic: Our house bore a debt beyond ordinary subjects; the blow tears out our vitals.

sentences.zh: 皇太子以丁酉踐酋號，哀喜交並，不知所措。

translations.literal: On dingyou the heir apparent ascended the throne; sorrow and joy intertwined—none knew how to behave.
translations.idiomatic: On the dingyou day the crown prince ascended the throne; grief and elation warred until no one knew how to stand.

sentences.zh: 吾身受顧命，輔相幼主，竊自揆度；

translations.literal: I personally received the deathbed charge to aid the young sovereign; privately I take my own measure.
translations.idiomatic: The dying sovereign named me regent over a child ruler; I weigh myself against the burden.

sentences.zh: 才非博陸而受姬公負圖之託，懼忝丞相輔漢之效；

translations.literal: My talent is no match for Huo Guang’s, yet I bear the chart-tablet charge once laid on the Duke of Zhou; I fear disgracing the precedent of Zhuge Liang’s stewardship of Han.
translations.idiomatic: I am no Huo Guang, yet I carry the Duke of Zhou’s yellow-chart mandate; I dread failing the standard Zhuge Liang set when he steadied Shu.

sentences.zh: 恐損先帝委付之明，是以憂慚惶惶，所慮萬端。

translations.literal: I fear to dim the late emperor’s lucid trust—hence anxiety and shame swarm; cares multiply without end.
translations.idiomatic: I dread staining his clear-eyed choice—so shame and fear swarm ten thousand ways.

sentences.zh: 且民惡其上，動見瞻觀，何時易哉？

translations.literal: Moreover the people resent those above them; every move faces scrutiny—when does it become easy?
translations.idiomatic: The mob always eyes the throne with suspicion—when does governing turn easy?

sentences.zh: 今以頑鈍之姿，處保傅之位，艱多智寡，任重謀淺，誰為唇齒？

translations.literal: Now with blunt wit I occupy tutor’s station—perils many, wisdom shallow—who will be my shield-mate?
translations.idiomatic: A dull man holds the heir’s tutorship—danger thick, counsel thin—who stands my partner?

sentences.zh: 近漢之世，燕、蓋交遘，有上官之變，以身值此，何敢怡豫邪？

translations.literal: Under Later Han Prince Yan of Langye allied with Princess Gai—turmoil like the Shangguan coup followed; facing such a season, how dare I seek comfort?
translations.idiomatic: Later Han watched Prince Liu Dan of Yan intrigue with Princess Gai until revolt boiled—the Shangguan crisis all over again; in such an hour who could rest easy?

sentences.zh: 又弟所在，與賊犬牙相錯，當於今時整頓軍具，率厲將士，警備過常，念出萬死，無顧一生，以報朝廷，無忝爾先。

translations.literal: Moreover where you stand, enemy lines mesh like dogs’ teeth; now you must sharpen weapons, steel the troops, redouble vigilance beyond the norm, resolve to die ten thousand deaths without sparing one life, to repay the court and shame not your forebears.
translations.idiomatic: Your sector teeth into Wei—you must drill arms, rouse men, watch harder than common duty, pledge ten thousand deaths for one life of service, pay the dynasty, honor the clan.

sentences.zh: 又諸將備守各有境界，猶恐賊虜聞諱，恣睢寇竊。

translations.literal: Further, each defending general holds his own sector—yet I fear the foe, hearing our mourning, will surge in reckless raids.
translations.idiomatic: Each commander guards a beat—yet Wei may hear our grief and raid.

sentences.zh: 邊邑諸曹，已別下約敕，所部督將，不得妄委所戍，逕來奔赴。

translations.literal: District offices already received separate orders: unit leaders must not rashly abandon their posts and dash homeward.
translations.idiomatic: County staff are warned: no colonel may bolt his wall and race to the capital.

sentences.zh: 雖懷愴但不忍之心，公義奪私，伯禽服戎，若苟違戾，非徒小故。

translations.literal: Though we cherish grief’s reluctance, public duty overrides private feeling—Bo Qin donned armor for the Rong; to disobey would be no small matter.
translations.idiomatic: Personal sorrow must yield—Bo Qin marched against the Rong though his heart tore; defiance would be grave crime.

sentences.zh: 以親正疏，古人明戒也。

translations.literal: Using kinship to correct estrangement is the plain lesson of antiquity.
translations.idiomatic: The ancients warned: kinship must mend division.

sentences.zh: 恪更拜太傅。

translations.literal: Ke was transferred to Grand Tutor.
translations.idiomatic: They elevated Ke to Grand Tutor.

sentences.zh: 於是罷視聽，息校官，原逋責，除關稅，事崇恩澤，眾莫不悅。

translations.literal: Thereupon surveillance posts were abolished, palace investigators idled, overdue levies forgiven, transit dues lifted—policy leaned on grace until none failed to rejoice.
translations.idiomatic: He killed informers, shelved spies, forgave arrears, lifted tolls—the reign ran on mercy and the realm sang.

sentences.zh: 恪每出入，百姓延頸思見其狀。

translations.literal: Whenever Ke went abroad commoners craned their necks hoping to glimpse his bearing.
translations.idiomatic: Every outing drew crowds straining for a sight of him.

sentences.zh: 恪遂有輕敵之心，以十二月戰克，明年春，復欲出軍。

translations.literal: Ke then grew contemptuous of the foe; though battle ended in victory that twelfth month, the next spring he wished to march again.
translations.idiomatic: December’s win went to his head; come spring he hungered for another campaign.

sentences.zh: 〈《漢晉春秋》曰：恪使司馬李衡往蜀說姜維，令同舉，曰：「古人有言，聖人不能為時，時至亦不可失也。

translations.literal: The Han Jin Chunqiu says: Ke sent Major Li Heng to Shu to persuade Jiang Wei to coordinate, saying, “The ancients observed that even sages cannot manufacture the hour—yet when the hour comes it must not be lost.”
translations.idiomatic: The Han Jin Chunqiu records Ke dispatching Li Heng to Jiang Wei: “Even sages cannot summon their moment—but they must seize it when it arrives.”

sentences.zh: 今敵政在私門，外內猜隔，兵挫於外，而民怨於內，自曹操以來，彼之亡形未有如今者也。

translations.literal: Now power sits in private cliques, inner and outer eye each other with suspicion, armies falter abroad while folk curse within—from Cao Cao onward their doom-signs have never matched today’s.
translations.idiomatic: Wei’s cords lie in cabals; court and camp mistrust each other; armies lose abroad, peasants curse within—never since Cao Cao has ruin stared so plain.

sentences.zh: 若大舉伐之，使吳攻其東，漢入其西，彼救西則東虛，重東則西輕，以練實之軍，乘虛輕之敵，破之必矣。

translations.literal: If we strike on a grand scale—Wu pressing their east while Han enters their west—they rescue west and east empties; weight east and west lightens; seasoned troops strike hollow, slack foes—victory is certain.
translations.idiomatic: A two-front storm—Wu on the east, Shu on the west—must overstretch them; veteran hosts hitting thin lines cannot lose.

sentences.zh: 」維從之。〉

translations.literal: Jiang Wei followed the plan.
translations.idiomatic: Jiang Wei agreed.

sentences.zh: 諸大臣以為數出罷勞，同辭諫恪，恪不聽。

translations.literal: Senior ministers deemed repeated expeditions exhausting and jointly remonstrated; Ke would not hear them.
translations.idiomatic: The council protested in one voice that serial campaigns broke men; Ke brushed them off.

sentences.zh: 中散大夫蔣延或以固爭，扶出。

translations.literal: Palace Gentleman Jiang Yan argued stubbornly and was dragged out.
translations.idiomatic: Jiang Yan, gentleman attendant, argued until guards hustled him away.

sentences.zh: 恪乃著論諭眾意曰：

translations.literal: Ke then composed a treatise to instruct popular opinion, saying:
translations.idiomatic: Ke answered with a manifesto:

sentences.zh: 夫天無二日，土無二王，王者不務兼併天下而欲垂祚後世，古今未之有也。

translations.literal: Heaven admits no second sun; earth bears no second king—never in antiquity or today has a true king aimed to pass down fortune without striving to swallow the realm.
translations.idiomatic: Two suns cannot share the sky; two kings cannot share the soil—no emperor ever secured his line without conquering all beneath it.

sentences.zh: 昔戰國之時，諸候自恃兵強地廣，互有救援，謂此足以傳世，人莫能危。

translations.literal: In the Warring States age each lord trusted his strong armies and broad lands, lent aid across borders, deemed such enough to preserve his line forever beyond peril.
translations.idiomatic: Warring States princes trusted mutual rescue and vast domains to live forever safe.

sentences.zh: 恣情從懷，憚於勞苦，使秦漸得自大，遂以並之，此既然矣。

translations.literal: They indulged whim and shrank from toil until Qin-by degrees grew paramount and annexed them—so it proved.
translations.idiomatic: They lounged while Qin grew—then swallowed them whole.

sentences.zh: 近者劉景昇在荊州，有眾十萬，財谷如山。

translations.literal: Recently Liu Jingsheng held Jingzhou with a hundred thousand men and grain piled like hills.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Biao once held Jingzhou—hosts in six figures, granaries like mountains.

sentences.zh: 不及曹操尚微，與之力競，坐觀其強大，吞滅諸袁，北方都定之後，操率三十萬眾來向荊州，當時雖有吞智者，不能復為畫計，於是景升兒子，交臂請降，遂為囚虜。

translations.literal: Before Cao Cao was still weak he declined to wrestle him, sat watching him swell, swallow the Yuans, settle the north—then Cao led three hundred thousand south toward Jingzhou; though wise men remained, none could sketch further counsel; Jingsheng’s sons folded arms and sued for surrender, ending prisoners.
translations.idiomatic: He refused to strike Cao while Cao was small, watched him crush the Yuans and pacify the north—then three hundred thousand Wei troops rolled south; even clever advisers could plot nothing; Biao’s sons surrendered shackled.

sentences.zh: 凡敵國欲相吞，即仇雠欲相除也，有仇而長之，禍不在己，則在後人，不可不為遠慮也。

translations.literal: Whenever rival states mean to devour each other it is as mortal foes meaning to erase each other—if you nurse an enemy you grow it; the calamity falls not on you then on those after—long sight cannot be neglected.
translations.idiomatic: States that would eat each other are feuds that must be killed—feed your foe and your heirs pay.

sentences.zh: 昔伍子胥曰：『越十年生聚，十年教訓，二十年之外，吳其為沼乎！

translations.literal: Wu Zixu said of old: “Yue will breed men ten years and train them ten years—twenty years hence Wu shall be marsh!”
translations.idiomatic: Wu Zixu warned: “Ten years Yue breeds men, ten years schools them—twenty years on, Wu becomes swamp!”

sentences.zh: 』夫差自恃強大，聞此邈然，是以誅子胥而無備越之心，至於臨敗悔之，豈有及乎？

translations.literal: Fucha trusted his might, heard this with lofty dismissiveness—therefore he executed Zixu and never prepared against Yue; only when ruin closed in did he repent—could that avail?
translations.idiomatic: Fucha trusted strength, sneered, slew Zixu, ignored Yue—too late he repented at the water’s edge.

sentences.zh: 越小於吳，尚為吳禍，況其強大者邪？

translations.literal: Yue was smaller than Wu yet became Wu’s scourge—how much more a greater power?
translations.idiomatic: Lesser Yue ruined Wu—what of a stronger foe?

sentences.zh: 昔秦但得關西耳，尚以併吞六國，今賊皆得秦趙、韓、魏、燕齊九州之地，地悉戎馬之鄉，士林之藪。

translations.literal: Antiquity’s Qin possessed only the ground west of the passes yet swallowed the six kingdoms; today’s rebels hold Guanzhong and the old domains of Zhao, Han, Wei, Yan, and Qi—the nine heartland provinces where every vale breeds chargers and every dell hides scholars.
translations.idiomatic: Classic Qin held only the western march yet devoured six states; Wei now owns Guanzhong and the Zhao-Han-Wei-Yan-Qi heartland—nine provinces of cavaliers and lettered men.

sentences.zh: 今以魏比古之秦，土地數倍；

translations.literal: Compare Wei to antique Qin—their territory multiples several fold.
translations.idiomatic: Wei beside classic Qin spans several times the ground.

sentences.zh: 以吳與蜀比古穴國，不能半之。

translations.literal: Compare Wu and Shu to ancient cave-minnow states—they do not reach half.
translations.idiomatic: Wu and Shu together are not half that footprint.

sentences.zh: 然所以能敵之，但以操時兵眾於今適盡，而後生者未悉長大，正是賊衰少未盛之時。

translations.literal: Yet we can oppose them only because Cao Cao’s veterans are largely spent while replacements have not yet grown—this is precisely the foe’s thinning hour before his zenith.
translations.idiomatic: We endure because Cao’s cohort died off and boys still train—the enemy trough before the crest.

sentences.zh: 加司馬懿先誅王淩，續自隕斃，其子幼弱，而專彼大任，雖有智計之士，未得施用。

translations.literal: Add that Sima Yi first executed Wang Ling then himself perished; his sons are young yet clutch supreme command—though strategists exist they cannot be employed.
translations.idiomatic: Sima Yi slew Wang Ling then died; weak sons hold supreme command—brains stay bottled.

sentences.zh: 當今伐之，是其厄會。

translations.literal: To strike now is to catch their crisis.
translations.idiomatic: Strike now and you hit the hinge moment.

sentences.zh: 聖人急於趨時，誠謂今日。

translations.literal: Sages hurry to ride the moment—I declare today that hour.
translations.idiomatic: The sage races time—I say that hour is today.

sentences.zh: 若順眾人之情，懷偷安之計，以為長江之險可以傳世；

translations.literal: If we follow the multitude’s mood and hug a policy of stolen ease, reckoning the Yangzi’s barrier enough to pass down generations —
translations.idiomatic: Follow the crowd, cling to false peace, trust the Long River as eternal shield—

sentences.zh: 不論魏之終始，而以今日遂輕其後。

translations.literal: without weighing Wei’s beginning and end yet lightly dismissing what follows today —
translations.idiomatic: —ignore Wei’s arc yet shrug at tomorrow—

sentences.zh: 此吾所以長歎息者也。

translations.literal: that is why I sigh long.
translations.idiomatic: that is why I groan aloud.

sentences.zh: 自本以來，務在產育，今者賊民歲月繁滋，但以尚小，未可得用耳。

translations.literal: From our founders day we have urged breeding population; now enemy folk multiply yearly—they are still young and not yet usable.
translations.idiomatic: Since dynastic founding we bred people; Wei’s peasants swell each year—they are young but not yet spear fodder.

sentences.zh: 若復十數年後，其眾必倍於今，而國家勁兵之地，皆已空盡，唯有此見眾可以定事。

translations.literal: Wait another dozen years and their numbers must double today’s while our elite regions already stand emptied—only these present troops can settle the matter.
translations.idiomatic: Another decade doubles their ranks while our crack districts hollow—only today’s soldiers can decide it.

sentences.zh: 若不早用之，端坐使老，復十數年，略當損半，而見子弟數不足言。

translations.literal: If we do not use them early but sit until they age, another decade will roughly halve them while our sons barely merit mention.
translations.idiomatic: Idle them till old age and ten years cuts our hosts in half while heirs thin to nothing.

sentences.zh: 若賊眾一倍，而我兵損半，雖復使伊、管圖之，未可如何。

translations.literal: If enemy strength doubles while ours halves, though Yi Yin and Guan Zhong plotted, nothing could be done.
translations.idiomatic: Double them and halve us—even Yi Yin and Guan Zhong could not save us.

sentences.zh: 今不達遠慮者，必以此言為迂。

translations.literal: Men lacking far sight must deem such words pedantic.
translations.idiomatic: Short thinkers will call this preachy.

sentences.zh: 夫禍難未至而豫憂慮，此固眾人之所迂也。

translations.literal: Calamity not yet arrived yet anxiety beforehand—this is what common minds dismiss as pedantic.
translations.idiomatic: Worry before disaster looks foolish—crowds always sneer.

sentences.zh: 及於難至，然後頓顙，雖有智者，又不能圖。

translations.literal: When disaster strikes they knock foreheads in vain—though wise men remain, nothing can be plotted.
translations.idiomatic: Disaster lands and they beat their brows—too late for even wise heads.

sentences.zh: 此乃古今所病，非獨一時。

translations.literal: This sickness runs through ages—not one moment alone.
translations.idiomatic: That folly spans every age—not ours alone.

sentences.zh: 昔吳始以伍員為迂，故難至而不可救。

translations.literal: Long ago Wu first deemed Wu Yuan pedantic—hence when calamity arrived they could not be saved.
translations.idiomatic: Wu once mocked Wu Zixu as alarmist—when doom came there was no remedy.

sentences.zh: 劉景升不能慮十年之後，故無以治其子孫。

translations.literal: Liu Jingsheng could not plan ten years ahead—therefore he had no way to govern his sons and grandsons.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Biao never looked past the decade—so he left no shelter for his heirs.

sentences.zh: 今恪無具臣之才，而受大吳蕭、霍之任，智與眾同思不經遠，若不及今日為國斥境，俯仰年老，而仇敵更強。

translations.literal: Now Ke lacks the talent of a mere competent minister yet bears Great Wu’s charge such as fell to Xiao He and Huo Guang; his wisdom matches the crowd’s and his thought does not reach far—if he does not today for the state push the frontier, in the blink of an eye he will age while foes grow stronger.
translations.idiomatic: I lack common bureaucratic polish yet carry a Xiao-Huo burden for Wu; my wit is ordinary—if I fail to widen our borders now, old age will creep in while enemies swell.

sentences.zh: 欲刎頸謝責，寧有補邪？

translations.literal: Wishing then to cut one’s throat and apologize for fault—would that avail?
translations.idiomatic: Would slitting my throat then undo the stain?

sentences.zh: 今聞眾人或以百姓尚貧，欲務閒息，此不右其慮其大危而其小勤者也。

translations.literal: Now I hear some argue that because the common people remain poor they wish to pursue ease and rest—this fails to weigh supreme peril against petty hardship.
translations.idiomatic: Some plead poverty and urge repose—they fret over small fatigue while ignoring existential peril.

sentences.zh: 昔漢祖幸已自有三秦之地，何不閉關守險以自娛樂，空出攻楚，身被創痍，介冑生蟣蝨，將士厭困苦，豈甘鋒刃而忘安寧哉？

translations.literal: Of old the Han Founding Emperor already possessed the Three Qins—why did he not bar the passes and guard the defiles for private pleasure, instead marching out empty-handed against Chu, his body scarred, lice breeding in helm and mail, officers sick of misery—did they relish naked blades and forget quiet?
translations.idiomatic: Gaozu held Guanzhong—why not bolt Hangu and feast? He chose war: wounds, lice in his armor, troops pushed past endurance—not because they loved steel over peace.

sentences.zh: 慮於長久不得兩存者耳！

translations.literal: They reckoned that long-term survival allowed no two powers side by side!
translations.idiomatic: They knew two dragons cannot share one pool.

sentences.zh: 每覽荊邯說公孫述以進取之圖，近風家叔父表陳與賊爭競之計，未嘗不喟然歎息也。

translations.literal: Whenever I read how Jing Han urged Gongsun Shu with plans of advance, or lately my uncle’s memorial laying out how to vie with the foe, never do I fail to sigh aloud.
translations.idiomatic: Each time I read Jing Han’s brief to Gongsun Shu or my uncle’s essay on tackling Wei, I groan with recognition.

sentences.zh: 夙夜反側，所慮如此，故聊疏愚言，以達二三君子之末。

translations.literal: Night and day I toss with such cares—therefore I loosely set forth these blunt words to reach the ears of you gentlemen.
translations.idiomatic: These worries cost me sleep—so I sketch this crude plea for you few who judge.

sentences.zh: 若一朝隕歿志畫不立，貴令來世知我所憂，可思於後。

translations.literal: If one morning I fall dead before designs are fixed, may later generations know what gnawed me and ponder it after.
translations.idiomatic: If I die before the plan is laid, let posterity read my fear and learn.

sentences.zh: 眾皆以恪此論欲必為之辭，然莫敢復難。

translations.literal: All deemed Ke’s discourse mere excuse for what he meant to do—yet none dared argue again.
translations.idiomatic: Courtiers saw the manifesto as a rubber stamp for war—and none spoke against him twice.

sentences.zh: 丹楊太守聶友素與恪善。

translations.literal: Nie You, governor of Danyang, had long been friendly with Ke.
translations.idiomatic: Nie You of Danyang was an old friend of Ke.

sentences.zh: 書諫恪曰：「大行皇帝本有遏東關之計，計未施行。

translations.literal: He wrote remonstrating Ke: “The late emperor originally planned to stem the foe at Dongguan—the plan was never executed.
translations.idiomatic: He warned Ke in a letter: “Your late lord meant to block Wei at Dongguan—that scheme never launched.

sentences.zh: 今公輔贊大業，成先帝之志。

translations.literal: Now as chief counselor you aid the great enterprise and fulfill the prior emperor’s intent.
translations.idiomatic: You now steward the realm—finish what he began.

sentences.zh: 寇遠自送，將士憑賴威德，出身用命，一旦有非常之功，豈非宗廟神靈社稷之福邪！

translations.literal: The foe has marched far to deliver themselves; officers lean on your awe and grace and stake lives on orders—should extraordinary merit arise in one stroke, would it not be fortune from ancestral spirits and altars of soil and grain?”
translations.idiomatic: The enemy walks into our fist; your army fights confident—one lightning strike could bless temple and state.”

sentences.zh: 宜且案兵養銳，觀釁而動。

translations.literal: For the moment stay arms and sharpen blades; watch for cracks then strike.
translations.idiomatic: Bide: rest the troops, hone steel, move only when heaven opens a seam.

sentences.zh: 今乘此勢欲復大出，天時未可。

translations.literal: Now riding this impulse you mean another grand expedition—the seasons forbid it.
translations.idiomatic: Another giant march now—the omens say no.

sentences.zh: 而苟任盛意，私心以為不安。

translations.literal: Yet if you indulge stubborn will, privately I count it unsafe.
translations.idiomatic: Yield to stubborn pride and I tremble for you.

sentences.zh: 」恪題論後，為書答友曰：「足下雖有自然之理，然未見大數。

translations.literal: Ke penned a postscript to his essay and replied to You: “Though you hold natural sense, you have not grasped the larger reckoning.
translations.idiomatic: Ke appended his tract and answered: “You speak prudence but miss the grand calculus.

sentences.zh: 熟省此論，可以開悟矣。

translations.literal: Peruse this argument closely—it should enlighten.”
translations.idiomatic: Read my paper twice—you will see.”

sentences.zh: 」於是違眾出軍，大發州郡二十萬眾，百姓騷動，始失人心。

translations.literal: Thereupon he defied consensus and took the field, levying two hundred thousand from provinces and commanderies; common folk churned and he first forfeited popular hearts.
translations.idiomatic: He marched against every voice and drafted two hundred thousand—panic spread and goodwill snapped.

sentences.zh: 恪意欲曜威淮南，驅略民人。

translations.literal: Ke intended to dazzle Huainan with might and drive off the populace as spoil.
translations.idiomatic: He meant to thunder across Huainan and herd Wei civilians as booty.

sentences.zh: 而諸將或難之曰：「今引軍深入，疆場之民，必相率遠遁，恐兵勞而功少，不如止圍新城。

translations.literal: Some generals objected: “Lead the army deep and border folk will flee in packs—we fear weary troops for slender gain; better halt and besiege Xincheng alone.
translations.idiomatic: His officers said: “Drive inland and every farmer flees—toil without loot; ring Xincheng instead.

sentences.zh: 新城困，救必至，至而圖之，乃可大獲。

translations.literal: When Xincheng is straitened relief must come—meet it then and you may reap hugely.”
translations.idiomatic: Siege Xincheng and relief columns will come—cut those and the harvest is rich.”

sentences.zh: 」恪從其計，回軍還圍新城。

translations.literal: Ke followed their plan, wheeled the army back, and invested Xincheng.
translations.idiomatic: Ke agreed, swung about, and threw trenches around Xincheng.

sentences.zh: 攻守連月，城不拔。

translations.literal: Attack and defense dragged months—the city did not fall.
translations.idiomatic: Month on month the walls stood.

sentences.zh: 士卒疲勞，因暑飲水，洩下、流腫，病者大半，死傷塗地。

translations.literal: Soldiers flagged; drinking warm summer water they suffered flux and limb swell—more than half fell sick, dead and wounded littered the ground.
translations.idiomatic: Heat and foul water brought dysentery and dropsy—half the host sick, corpses strewn like cordwood.

sentences.zh: 諸營吏日白病者多，恪以為作，欲斬之，自是莫敢言。

translations.literal: Camp clerks daily reported many sick; Ke judged it feigned and threatened execution—after that none dared speak.
translations.idiomatic: Daily sick lists drew his suspicion of malingering—after one death threat silence fell.

sentences.zh: 恪內惟失計，而恥城不下，忿形於色。

translations.literal: Within Ke knew his plan had failed; shamed that the city stood, rage showed on his face.
translations.idiomatic: He knew he had blundered yet could not bear the insult of stalled siege—wrath carved his brow.

sentences.zh: 將軍朱異有所是非，恪怒，立奪其兵。

translations.literal: General Zhu Yi spoke critically; Ke in fury instantly stripped him of command.
translations.idiomatic: Zhu Yi criticized him—Ke seized his troops on the spot.

sentences.zh: 都尉蔡林數陳軍計，恪不能用，策馬奔魏。

translations.literal: Commandant Cai Lin repeatedly offered stratagems; Ke ignored him, so Lin spurred his horse and fled to Wei.
translations.idiomatic: Cai Lin pled tactics in vain—he bolted to Wei.

sentences.zh: 魏知戰士罷病，乃進救兵。

translations.literal: Wei learned the warriors were spent and sick, then pushed relief troops forward.
translations.idiomatic: Wei saw Wu wilting and threw in reinforcements.

sentences.zh: 恪引軍而去。

translations.literal: Ke led the army away.
translations.idiomatic: Ke broke camp and withdrew.

sentences.zh: 士卒傷病，流曳道路，或頓僕坑壑，或見略獲，存記忿痛，大小呼嗟。

translations.literal: Wounded and ill soldiers dragged along the roads—some collapsed in ditches, some were seized; survivors nursed rage and pain, great and small wailing.
translations.idiomatic: The retreat was a trail of cripples—some dropped in gullies, some were captured; groans followed Ke home.

sentences.zh: 而恪宴然自若。

translations.literal: Yet Ke remained placid as if nothing were wrong.
translations.idiomatic: Ke himself looked unruffled.

sentences.zh: 出住江渚一月，圖起田於潯陽，詔召相銜，徐乃旋師。

translations.literal: He moved out to dwell on the river islets a full month, plotting to open fields at Xunyang; edicts summoned him in relays—only slowly did he wheel the army back.
translations.idiomatic: He camped a month on the Yangzi flats, mumbling about reclamation at Xunyang while summons stacked—then drifted homeward.

sentences.zh: 由此眾庶失望，而怨黷興矣。

translations.literal: From this the multitude despaired and grievance flared.
translations.idiomatic: Hope curdled into open hatred.

sentences.zh: 秋八月軍還，陳兵導從，歸入府館。

translations.literal: In autumn, eighth month, the army returned; he paraded troops as escort and entered his mansion.
translations.idiomatic: That eighth month he marched home with full panoply into his regency hall.

sentences.zh: 即召中書令孫嘿，厲聲謂曰：「卿等何敢妄數作詔？

translations.literal: He immediately summoned Palace Secretariat Director Sun Hei and barked, “How dare you scribble edicts at whim?”
translations.idiomatic: He hauled in Sun Hei and snarled, “Who authorized these endless edicts?”

sentences.zh: 」嘿惶懼辭出，因病還家。

translations.literal: Hei fled in terror, pleaded illness, and retired home.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Hei bolted, then claimed sickness and hid.

sentences.zh: 恪徵行之後，曹所奏署令長職司，一罷更選，愈治威嚴，多所罪責，當進見者無不竦息。

translations.literal: After Ke set out on campaign every magistrate and bureau chief the council had appointed—he cashiered the lot and reappointed, ruling with fiercer awe and heavier blame; none who faced audience failed to tremble.
translations.idiomatic: Every official picked while he was gone was purged and replaced; audiences became gauntlets of terror.

sentences.zh: 又改易宿衛，用其親近。

translations.literal: He reshuffled the palace guard for his own intimates.
translations.idiomatic: The inner guard was swapped for his creatures.

sentences.zh: 復敕兵嚴，欲向責、徐。

translations.literal: He again ordered troops readied, aiming toward Huang and Xu.
translations.idiomatic: He mobilized anew—eyes on Huangzhou and Xuzhou.

sentences.zh: 孫峻因民之多怨，眾之所嫌，構恪欲為變，與亮謀，置酒請恪。

translations.literal: Sun Jun, exploiting popular resentment and collective loathing, framed Ke as plotting revolt; conspiring with Liang he set wine and invited Ke.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Jun rode the hatred, whispered coup to Liang, and baited Ke with a banquet.

sentences.zh: 恪將見之夜，精爽擾動，通夕不寐。

translations.literal: The night Ke was to attend, his spirit felt shaken and he lay awake till dawn.
translations.idiomatic: The eve of the feast his nerves jangled—no sleep.

sentences.zh: 明將盥漱，聞水腥臭，侍者授衣，衣服亦臭。

translations.literal: At dawn as he washed the water stank of blood; attendants handed robes that likewise reeked.
translations.idiomatic: Wash water smelled of gore; fresh robes brought the same stench.

sentences.zh: 恪怪其故，易衣易水，其臭如初，意惆悵不悅。

translations.literal: Ke wondered at the cause; changing water and clothes, the stench remained as before—his heart sank.
translations.idiomatic: New water, new silk—the rot persisted—unease gnawed him.

sentences.zh: 嚴畢趨出，太銜引其衣，恪曰：「犬不欲我行乎？

translations.literal: When dress was done he hurried out; his dog seized his robe—Ke said, “Does the dog forbid my going?”
translations.idiomatic: As he left for court his dog gripped his sleeve—“Do you bar my road?” he asked.

sentences.zh: 」還坐，頃刻乃復起，犬又銜其衣，恪令從者逐犬，遂升車。

translations.literal: He returned to sit; presently rose again—the dog seized his robe once more; Ke ordered followers to drive off the dog and mounted his carriage.
translations.idiomatic: He sat, rose—the dog pulled again; servants chased it off and he rolled toward the palace.

sentences.zh: 初，恪將徵淮南，有孝子著縗衣入其閣中，從者白之，令外詰問，孝子曰：「不自覺入。

translations.literal: Earlier, when Ke was bound for Huainan, a filial son in mourning hemp entered his chamber; attendants reported it and he had him questioned outside—the mourner said, “I did not realize I had entered.”
translations.idiomatic: Before the Huainan march a man in mourning drifted into his hall—“I wandered in unaware,” he said under questioning.

sentences.zh: 」時中外守備，亦悉不見，眾皆異之。

translations.literal: At the time inner and outer guards saw nothing extraordinary—all deemed it uncanny.
translations.idiomatic: Guards saw nothing—everyone called it an omen.

sentences.zh: 出行之後，所坐廳事屋棟中折。

translations.literal: After he marched the ridgebeam of his audience hall snapped.
translations.idiomatic: Once he left, the main hall ridgebeam cracked.

sentences.zh: 自新城出住東興，有白虹見其船，還拜蔣陵，白虹復繞其車。

translations.literal: From Xincheng he shifted to Dongxing—a white rainbow spanned his boat; returning he worshipped at Jiang Mausoleum and a white rainbow wrapped his cart.
translations.idiomatic: A white arc bridged his ship at Dongxing; another haloed his carriage at imperial tombs.

sentences.zh: 及將見，駐車宮門，峻已伏兵於帷中，恐恪不時入，事洩，自出見恪曰：「使君若尊體不安，自可須後，峻當具白主上。

translations.literal: When about to enter audience he halted his carriage at the palace gate—Jun had already hidden troops behind curtains; fearing Ke might not enter on schedule and the plot leak, Jun came out himself and said to Ke, “If Your Honor feels unwell you may wait—I shall report fully to our lord.”
translations.idiomatic: At the palace gate Jun—troops already hidden—stepped out lest Ke turn back: “If you are ill, delay; I will explain to the throne.”

sentences.zh: 」欲以嘗知恪。

translations.literal: He meant thereby to probe Ke’s mind.
translations.idiomatic: He was sounding Ke’s nerve.

sentences.zh: 恪答曰：「當自力入。

translations.literal: Ke answered, “I shall force myself to enter.”
translations.idiomatic: “I will attend,” Ke said.

sentences.zh: 」散騎常侍張約、朱恩等密書與恪曰：「今日張設非常，疑有他故。

translations.literal: Palace Gentlemen Zhang Yue and Zhu En secretly wrote Ke: “Today’s arrangement is extraordinary—I suspect another purpose.”
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Yue and Zhu En slipped a note: “Something is wrong with tonight’s layout.”

sentences.zh: 」恪省書而去。

translations.literal: Ke read the letter and went on.
translations.idiomatic: Ke skimmed it and still walked in.

sentences.zh: 未出路門，逢太常滕胤，恪曰：「卒腹痛，不任人。

translations.literal: Before reaching the outer gate he met Chamberlain for Ceremonies Teng Yin—Ke said, “Sudden belly pain—I cannot bear company.”
translations.idiomatic: Outside he met Teng Yin—“Stomach cramps—I should turn back,” Ke claimed.

sentences.zh: 」胤不知峻陰計，謂恪曰：「君自行旋未見，今上酒請君，君已至門，宜當力進。

translations.literal: Yin did not know Jun’s secret plot and said to Ke, “Since Your Lordship returned you have not been summoned to court; now His Majesty holds wine for you—you have reached the gate—you ought press forward.”
translations.idiomatic: Yin, ignorant of the trap, urged him: “The boy emperor waits with wine—you are at the door—go.”

sentences.zh: 」恪躊躇而還，劍履上殿。

translations.literal: Ke hesitated but returned, ascending the hall sword and slippers permitted.
translations.idiomatic: He wavered, then climbed the steps armed—a privilege few enjoyed.

sentences.zh: 謝亮，還坐。

translations.literal: He thanked Liang and resumed his seat.
translations.idiomatic: He bowed to Sun Liang and sat.

sentences.zh: 設酒，恪疑未飲，峻因曰：「使君病未善平，當有常服藥酒，自可取之。

translations.literal: Wine was poured; Ke hesitated to drink—Jun said, “Your Honor’s illness is not quite eased—you must keep medicinal wine—fetch your own.”
translations.idiomatic: Jun saw him hesitate: “Take your usual tonic wine—bring what you trust.”

sentences.zh: 」恪意乃安，別飲所齎酒。

translations.literal: Ke’s mind eased; he drank separately the wine he had brought.
translations.idiomatic: Reassured, he sipped only his private flask.

sentences.zh: 〈《吳曆》曰：張約、朱恩密疏告恪，恪以示滕胤，胤勸恪還，恪曰：「峻小子何能為邪！

translations.literal: The Wu li says: Zhang Yue and Zhu En sent a secret memorial warning Ke; Ke showed it to Teng Yin—Yin urged Ke to withdraw—Ke said, “What can young Jun accomplish?
translations.idiomatic: Wu li records the warning memo; Teng Yin begged retreat—“Jun is nothing,” Ke sneered.

sentences.zh: 但恐因酒食中人耳。

translations.literal: “I only fear poison slipped into food and drink.”
translations.idiomatic: “Worst case—spiked cups.”

sentences.zh: 」乃以藥酒入。

translations.literal: Thereupon he entered bearing medicinal wine.
translations.idiomatic: So he entered carrying his drug wine.

sentences.zh: 孫盛評曰：恪與胤親厚，約等疏，非常大事，勢應示胤，共謀安危。

translations.literal: Sun Sheng comments: Ke was intimate with Yin yet distant from Yue and company—for an event so grave he ought to have shown Yin and plotted survival together.
translations.idiomatic: Sun Sheng: Ke trusted Yin, not the warners—a coup deserved joint counsel.

sentences.zh: 然恪性強梁，加素侮峻，自不信，故入，豈胤微勸，便為之冒禍乎？

translations.literal: Yet Ke’s nature was overbearing and he habitually insulted Jun—he trusted himself—therefore he entered; could Yin’s mild hint make him brave catastrophe?
translations.idiomatic: Ke bullied Jun and trusted himself—would one soft word from Yin send him into the trap?

sentences.zh: 吳曆為長。〉

translations.literal: The Wu li account is superior.
translations.idiomatic: The Wu li version rings true.

sentences.zh: 酒數行，亮還內，峻起如廁，解長衣，著短服，出曰：「有詔收諸葛恪！」

translations.literal: After several rounds of wine Liang withdrew within; Jun rose as if to the privy, shed his long robe for short dress, emerged and cried, “Edict—to seize Zhuge Ke!”
translations.idiomatic: Mid-feast Liang slipped away; Jun returned in short jacket—“Arrest Zhuge Ke—by imperial order!”

sentences.zh: 〈《吳錄》曰：峻提刀稱詔收恪，亮起立曰：「非我所為！

translations.literal: The Wu lu says: Jun raised a blade, proclaimed the edict to seize Ke—Liang sprang up crying, “It was not I!
translations.idiomatic: Wu lu: Jun waved steel—Liang cried, “Not my doing!

sentences.zh: 非我所為！

translations.literal: It was not I!
translations.idiomatic: Not my doing!

sentences.zh: 」乳母引亮還內。

translations.literal: A wet nurse led Liang back within.
translations.idiomatic: Nurses hustled the boy emperor inside.

sentences.zh: 《吳曆》云：峻先引亮入，然後出稱詔。

translations.literal: The Wu li states: Jun first ushered Liang in, then emerged proclaiming the edict.
translations.idiomatic: Wu li says Jun hid Liang first, then announced the warrant.

sentences.zh: 與本傳同。

translations.literal: This matches the main biography.
translations.idiomatic: That agrees with this biography.

sentences.zh: 臣松之以為峻欲稱詔，宜如本傳及《吳曆》，不得如《吳錄》所言。〉

translations.literal: Your servant Pei Songzhi judges that if Jun wished to proclaim an edict it should follow this biography and the Wu li—not as the Wu lu relates.
translations.idiomatic: Pei Songzhi: a staged edict should match the main text and Wu li, not Wu lu.

sentences.zh: 恪驚起，拔劍未得，而峻刀交下。

translations.literal: Ke started up but before drawing his sword Jun’s blades crossed upon him.
translations.idiomatic: Ke leapt—steel met him before his sword cleared.

sentences.zh: 張約從旁斫峻，裁傷左手，峻應手斫約斷右臂。

translations.literal: Zhang Yue hacked at Jun from the side, barely wounding the left hand—Jun struck back and severed Yue’s right arm.
